Transcript body:
[00:00] Morgan (Redwood AE): hey everybody, thanks for joining. we'll try to keep this tight, 30-ish minutes of bench discussion then next steps. Samir, do you want to kick off with any high-level goals?
[00:08] Samir (Brightlane): yeah thanks Morgan. main goal for this week is to understand where Redwood sits vs the baseline provider on latency for our generative route and whether the batching + cache stuff actually helps on our workloads. also curious about tail latency since our production SLAs care about p95.
[00:23] Priya (Redwood SE): great. quick reminder of the baseline numbers we were given last week: baseline provider (we'll call them "base") was reporting about 45 req/s sustained at concurrency 16 for that prompt set, p50 ~120ms, p95 ~420ms per request in their published run. our goal was to match or beat p95 while keeping cost in check.
[00:45] Lina (SRE): just to clarify, those numbers are end-to-end request latencies including network and request parsing right? not pure token generation?
[00:52] Morgan: correct, includes end-to-end. for fairness we tried to run similar client-to-endpoint network patterns.
[00:58] Priya: ok jumping into our week-3 results. summary first: with default hosted config (no dedicated), using model redwood-variant-xq, continuous batching enabled, our sustained throughput hit ~92 req/s at concurrency 16, p50 65ms, p95 185ms on the same prompt set. with KV-cache off those numbers were about 70 req/s, p95 250ms. (note: deliberate slight transcription fuzziness in numbers).
[01:28] Tom (Data Eng): whoa 92 req/s that's double baseline. what's the token length distribution there? our prompts avg ~350 tokens incl. system messages.
[01:35] Priya: yes tokens were about 300-400 per request. the main wins came from two things: 1) our kernel selection + attention optimization for that architecture and sequence length distribution, 2) prefix/KV cache playback for repeated system prompts cut a lot of repeated compute.
[02:00] Evan (Infra): and also continuous batching strategy — we allowed small batching windows tuned to keep latency under 200ms while aggregating micro-batches. that reduced per-token overhead.
[02:14] Ava (PM): can you explain the KV-cache playback? is that safe with our data constraints?
[02:20] Priya: KV-cache is basically caching the key/value states for repeated prefixes so the model doesn't recompute attention for unchanged context. for your PII constraints, we can support cache scoping and TTL and also encrypt caches at rest. works with VPC private deployments too.
[02:38] Samir: numbers look promising. can you give breakdown of where p95 time is spent? I want to see kernel time vs network vs queueing.
[02:45] Priya: sure. quick breakdown from the run: average compute kernel time ~70ms, queueing/wait for batch ~30ms, network/serialization ~40ms, overhead for request handling ~45ms. total ~185ms. on the baseline, kernel time was higher due to unoptimized kernels and no KV cache; they were more like 180ms kernel + 70ms queueing + 70ms net = ~420ms.
[03:12] Lina: those are helpful. how reproducible are those p95 numbers? did you run multiple seeds / windows?
[03:18] Priya: we ran three separate 10-minute sustained runs and saw p95 vary between 170-205ms — so fairly stable. transcription note: one run had a small spike due to background infra update but we excluded it from primary numbers.
[03:33] Morgan: we also ran a dedicated-capacity simulation (reserved GPU pool) for shorter windows: that improved p95 to ~120ms with identical prompts because queueing dropped to single-digit ms. but that run cost estimate is higher — we included cost delta in the CSV we sent.
[03:50] Tom: can you share the CSV again? we didn't get the latest histograms.
[03:54] Morgan: yes will re-send. action: I'll put the run CSV + histograms in the shared folder and call out the flags used (batch size, micro-batching delay, kv-cache TTL).
[04:03] Samir: about quantization — we had a hypothesis the baseline was using int8/4 quant which might affect quality. did you try quantized kernels?
[04:11] Priya: we tested 8-bit quant profiles. throughput improved ~10-15% and kernel time dropped ~12ms, but we did see a small quality delta on a few red-team prompts. we flagged those in the evals. For now recommended: use 8-bit on non-critical routes and stick to FP16 for QA-sensitive traffic.
[04:33] Ava: quality delta — can you point to examples? we need that to sign off with product.
[04:37] Priya: yes we'll include a short eval diff file in the shared link (e.g., prompt ids 12, 47, 83).
[04:45] Ben (CSM): quick note on observability — you asked about token-level cost breakdowns and per-route traces. the console will show token cost by model and per-request spans if you enable tracing; we'll share a 21-day demo snapshot.
[04:57] Lina: are audit logs and KMS usage included in the private deployment? legal wants to confirm SOC 2 logging and HSM/KMS integration.
[05:05] Evan: yes private has KMS integrations + audit log export; SOC2 stuff is covered by our enterprise package. we'll attach the compliance pack.
[05:13] Samir: cool. couple more specifics on the benchmark: what workload shape causes worst tail? is it bursty or gradual increase?
[05:19] Priya: for your workload the worst tail was caused by short bursts where queueing temporarily spikes; micro-batching window tuning mitigated that. we recommend an autoscaler policy that pre-warms additional workers when RPS trend rises above threshold.
[05:33] Tom: on the dedicated run, what's the hardware baseline? you mentioned A100 equivalent.
[05:37] Morgan: we used A100S 80GB equiv for the dedicated simulation. we'll note exact instance types in the CSV.
[05:44] Ava: curious about cost comparison. at 92 req/s hosted vs 45 req/s base, is unit cost per token lower?
[05:49] Priya: good question. raw unit compute cost is comparable, but batching + KV cache reduced effective tokens processed per request which lowers overall billable token units — so your unit cost dropped ~18% in our sample. the dedicated run has lower per-token cost but higher fixed monthly commit.
[06:09] Samir: okay that maps to our thinking. next, any caveats on reproducibility across regions? we have EU and US tenants.
[06:15] Evan: perf differences across regions are minimal once you're on matched hardware; the main variable is network egress. we'll run EU-specific tests if you want.
[06:23] Morgan: quick question to the team: are we comfortable recommending a canary with hosted first and fall back to dedicated if tail persists?
[06:29] Priya: yes that's the suggested path: start hosted with tuned batching/KV cache and 8-bit selectively, monitor p95; if tail SLA not met, move to dedicated and re-run bench.
[06:39] Samir: sounds good. specific asks from our side: 1) raw CSV + latency hist, 2) run config and flags, 3) example eval diffs for quantization.
[06:49] Morgan: will do. I'll send that by Friday (2025-03-14).
[06:53] Ava: also need a short note on compliance (SOC2 + KMS) for our legal — can you attach that?
[06:58] Ben: yes we'll attach Redwood enterprise compliance pack and contact for security review.
[07:03] Tom: final technical Q — can we reproduce the KV-cache behavior on-prem if we choose private deployment?
[07:09] Priya: yes, KV-cache is part of the runtime and works with private. you'll need to coordinate cache storage path and encryption keys; we have a deployment checklist for on-prem.
[07:18] Samir: alright let's recap.
[07:20] Morgan: recap: send CSV + histograms + run flags + eval diffs (Priya/Morgan). schedule dedicated run for 2025-03-18 (Morgan). customer to send production prompt subset by 2025-03-16 (Tom). Redwood to add KV-cache playback scenario and re-run p95 test (Priya). attach compliance pack (Ben).
[07:43] Ava: thanks all, this was helpful.
[07:46] Morgan: thanks everyone, we'll follow up in the shared folder and send invites.
